newsitem.title: POLAND: NATO entry will benefit Polish economy - minister.
newsitem.headline: NATO entry will benefit Polish economy - minister.

text.p: NATO entry will stimulate Poland's economy, despite the costs of upgrading the armed forces, because it will attract foreign investors and high technology, Finance Minister Marek Belka said on Wednesday.
"Poland in NATO will be perceived as a more secure and more stable country, which will attract more investors..., especially investors bringing in high technology," Belka told a news briefing.

He said Poland's national budget was able to bear the direct costs of making the armed forces inter-operational with the pact's command, air space management and other procedures, which analysts put at $100-$150 million annually during the next several years.

"Modernising the army's equipment will of course be more expensive, but these costs would have to borne anyway," Belka said, adding that according to military analysts the costs were likely to total $11-$19 billion, spread over many years.

Poland, the Czech Repubic and Hungary have been named by the United States as the only countries from the former Soviet bloc to be invited to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation at its July 8-9 summit in Madrid.
The three countries could enter the pact in 1999 if parliaments of all the Western military alliance's states ratify the enlargement. The pact can meanwhile invite further countries to join.
Belka said he was confident a cost-cutting plan, being prepared by the defence ministry and the chief-of-staff, would allow the armed forces to generate means to purchase new, modern equipment.
The plan involves cutting the armed forces' personnel to 180,000 from the current 230,000 and getting rid of some old defence equipment.
Belka also said the economy would benefit from the restructuring and eventual privatisation of the often-ailing arms industry, which NATO entry would probably trigger.

Some Western arms makers, such as the U.S. Lockheed Martin and McDonnell Douglas and France's Dassault Aviation, have already announced proposals for industrial co-operation with the Polish defence sector, hoping to improve their chances in a planned tender for a supplier of multi-task fighter aircraft.
The government says Poland needs to replace about 100 of its 460 Soviet-made jets.
